cells.tense: Here, with the pen, the pieces are brought into one order that holds.
cells.act: return the small thing you owe before anyone asks
cells.ask: Think of a debt you've been carrying toward someone you care for — a reply, a borrowed book. Settle it before they ask.
cells.core:
The pieces of a life — what you owe, what you're tending, what needs answering — can be brought into an order that holds. You have that. What was scattered becomes one thing, and the one thing serves what's alive in your hands. The care isn't frantic; it's held.

Try it once, small. Choose a debt from the pile and settle it — a reply, a book to return. You'll know which one without working it out; your own sense of what's fair points at it. Pay it before anyone asks, and say nothing after. What you notice is the whole load getting lighter by one piece, and the lightness is the part you get to keep.
cells.sheetLine: You gather the pieces into one.
cells.place: where you care for what is growing

cells.tense: The future is being braced against, and the pieces are pulled toward it.
cells.act: move at the pace your feeling can sustain
cells.ask: Take one piece of what you're tending. Work it at a rhythm you could keep for a month — the speed your body allows, not the plan's.
cells.core:
Where you care for what's growing, the gathering runs ahead. The whole plan is already assembled, and the small living things are being pulled toward the shape you decided they'd take. What's young gets measured against what it should be by now. The pace is set by a future that hasn't arrived, so today lands late.

Find the rhythm that will still be there when you're tired. Take one piece of what you tend and work it at that speed. Leave the rest of the pile alone. The part of you wanting the whole harvest isn't wrong about the harvest; it's wrong about the day. The gait you can keep is the one that carries you there.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that closed behind you already.
cells.act: spend an hour with the thing you love without a task attached to it
cells.ask: Sit with something you love and bring no task. A garden, a person, a piece of music. Let the hour be only that.
cells.core:
You know what's owed, what needs lining up, what the next move is — and none of it has a hand in what's actually growing near you. What you're holding stays held. The care keeps arriving as thought instead of contact, and the thing your attention would have fed goes on growing without it.

No more gathering will bring it back. Instead, spend an hour with something you love and bring no task. A garden, a person, a piece of music. Let the hour be only that. You don't need to feel anything or learn anything. Contact starts when something is simply allowed to be near you again, unattended.
cells.sheetLine: What you hold stays held, and nothing gets your hands.
cells.place: where you care for what is growing

cells.tense: The pen is down, and the pages being written are not signed.
cells.act: let the gladness go out to the room
cells.ask: When something goes well with what you're growing, say so to whoever was part of it, the day it happens.
cells.core:
In this place the pieces really are coming into one order — a person steadied, a good next step chosen, a thing brought to the right hands — and the story afterward is luck or the season. The work of pulling it together is happening, and no one, including you, is counting it as done by you. What's cared for gets the benefit. What arranged it stays unthanked.

Let the gladness out instead. When something goes well, say so to whoever else was in it, the day it happens. One sentence is a celebration. Saying it out loud puts the credit where the work was, and it hands the good thing to the people who helped carry it.
cells.sheetLine: The good thing lands, and no one marks it.
cells.place: where you care for what is growing

attempts.check: The one claim the record cannot support is that the person is 'building the work of care for good.' The record shows the gathering is alive and the seat is right; it does not say the person has integrated the gatherer. A reader may reasonably say the scattered gathering and the chosen tending are one life, not two guests. The ask survives being wrong: it is a visible, one-time check-in on one person that costs nothing and stands on its own. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is 'The one who cares is the gatherer' — it flatters the mechanism into a profession the record never named.
